meta.title: India Economic Indicators 2014-2030
meta.author: Dr. Varna Sri Raman
meta.notes: Series are annual unless stated. Observed values run through 2026 and reflect the latest official releases retrieved by 10 October 2026 (MoSPI national accounts with the 2025-26 Provisional Estimate, PLFS Monthly Bulletin August 2026, Union Budget 2026-27, CPI August 2026, World Inequality Lab Working Paper 2024/09). One caveat carries across the whole CPI series: MoSPI replaced the 2012=100 index with a 2024=100 index from the January 2026 print, reweighted on HCES 2023-24, so the 2026 inflation figure is not on the same basis as 2014-2025 (see sources.cpiInflation). All values in the 'economic' block are observed (2014-2026); there is no projected year in this block. The 'forecast' block drives the Economic Trajectory tab: these are scenario projections to 2030, and none of them is a prediction. Every assumption is a choice, and every one is documented. Primer datasets (bigPicture, taxTake, spendSplit, stateReturns, realInflation, external, distribution, structure, chinaDivergence, jobsLesson) are drawn from the 'Reading the Indian Economy' citizen primer (16 June 2026).

sources.gdpGrowth: Real GDP growth, MoSPI national accounts. Year Y is the fiscal year that starts in April of Y (2014 = 2014-15), the same convention as the World Bank series used for 2004-2013. 2014-2022: the latest MoSPI estimates on the 2011-12 base (2017-18 6.8, 2018-19 6.5, 2019-20 3.9, 2020-21 -5.8, 2021-22 9.7, 2022-23 7.6). 2023-2025: the new series on base 2022-23. MoSPI's release of 27 February 2026 gives 2023-24 7.2 and 2024-25 7.1; the Provisional Estimates of 5 June 2026 give 2025-26 7.7 (7.8% was the fourth quarter alone). MoSPI's API returned 7.3, 7.2 and 7.8 for the same years and is not used; on the old base 2023-24 had been 9.2 and 2024-25 6.5. BASIS BREAK at 2023. 2026 (2026-27) is empty: the first annual estimate is due in January 2027. Quarterly growth for April to June 2026 was 7.8%. The World Bank series for 2004-2013 is on the 2011-12 base.
sources.unemployment: 2014-2025: annual rates on usual status (ps+ss). From 2017 a year is the PLFS survey year that starts in July of it (2017 = 2017-18), through 2023 (2023-24); 2024 and 2025 are MoSPI's calendar-year rates. 2026: the average of the 9 PLFS Monthly Bulletins published for 2026 (January to September 2026: January 5, February 4.9, March 5.1, April 5.2, May 5.5, June 5.5, July 5.1, August 5, September 5), all-India, persons 15+, rural + urban. BASIS BREAK: the monthly bulletins report current weekly status (CWS), which counts a person as unemployed on the past week's activity and runs well above usual status. The 2026 value is therefore a different measure from the years before it, and most of the rise from 3.1 per cent in 2025 is the change of measure. On the same weekly measure MoSPI's calendar-year rate for 2025 was 5.3 per cent.
sources.youthUnemployment: MoSPI PLFS, usual status (ps+ss), persons aged 15-29, all-India, rural + urban, from api.mospi.gov.in (retrieved 10 October 2026). 2017-2023 are the PLFS survey years starting in July of the year shown (2017 = 2017-18); 2024 and 2025 are MoSPI's calendar-year rates. 2014-2016 are left empty because PLFS began in 2017-18 and no comparable published figure exists. 2026 is left empty until an annual figure is published: the 2026 monthly bulletins average 15.3% for January to September, but they report current weekly status, which runs well above usual status.
sources.graduateUnemployment: MoSPI PLFS, usual status (ps+ss), persons aged 15 and over with a graduate degree, all-India, rural + urban, from api.mospi.gov.in (retrieved 10 October 2026). 2017-2023 are the PLFS survey years starting in July of the year shown (2017 = 2017-18). MoSPI publishes no figure for graduates for 2014-2016 (before PLFS) or for 2024 onward yet, so those years are left empty.
sources.top1Share: World Inequality Lab: Bharti, Chancel, Piketty and Somanchi (2024), 'Income and Wealth Inequality in India, 1922-2023', WIL Working Paper 2024/09, Statistical Appendix, table of per-adult pre-tax national income shares, 1951-2022. The series ends at 2022 (2022-23); 2023-2026 are empty because no annual figure has been published for them. Top 1% share.
sources.bottom50Share: World Inequality Lab: Bharti, Chancel, Piketty and Somanchi (2024), 'Income and Wealth Inequality in India, 1922-2023', WIL Working Paper 2024/09, Statistical Appendix, table of per-adult pre-tax national income shares, 1951-2022. The series ends at 2022 (2022-23); 2023-2026 are empty because no annual figure has been published for them. Bottom 50% share. The share fell to 13.9 in 2017, rose to 15.5 in 2020 and stood at 15.0 in 2022.
sources.formalEmployment: Derived from MoSPI PLFS published tables (api.mospi.gov.in, retrieved 10 October 2026), usual status (ps+ss), all-India, persons: the share of regular wage/salaried workers among all workers, multiplied by the share of regular wage/salaried employees with any social security benefit (100 minus the published share without any). 2017-18: 22.8% x 50.4% = 11.5; 2018-19: 23.8 x 48.1 = 11.4; 2019-20: 22.9 x 45.8 = 10.5; 2020-21: 21.1 x 46.2 = 9.7; 2021-22: 21.5 x 47.0 = 10.1; 2022-23: 20.9 x 46.1 = 9.6; 2023-24: 21.7 x 46.6 = 10.1. The social security table covers regular wage/salaried employees in the non-agricultural sector; regular wage work in agriculture is about 1% of workers. Years are PLFS survey years starting in July of the year shown. 2014-2016 (before PLFS) and 2024 onward (no annual table yet) are left empty.
sources.informalEmployment: 100 minus formalEmployment, for the years formalEmployment has a value.
sources.pressFreedom: Reporters Without Borders, World Press Freedom Index (annual). RSF published a single 2011-12 index; its rank (131) is shown for both 2011 and 2012. RSF ranked 167 to 179 countries in 2004-2013 and 180 since.
sources.fiscalDeficit: Union Budget documents; central government fiscal deficit as % of GDP, for the fiscal year starting in the year shown (2014 = 2014-15). 2025 is the provisional actual for 2025-26 released by the Controller General of Accounts on 1 June 2026 (Rs 15,19,169 crore, 4.4% of GDP); 2026 has no outturn yet. The Budget Estimate for 2026-27 (4.3, Union Budget of 1 February 2026) is held in the estimates block and drawn as a hollow marker; no average uses it.
sources.cpiInflation: MoSPI CPI (Combined), year-on-year. 2026: the average of the 9 monthly prints published for 2026 (January to September 2026: January 2.74, February 3.21, March 3.4, April 3.48, May 3.93, June 4.38, July 4.45, August 4.83, September 5.54). BASIS BREAK: from the January 2026 print (published 12 Feb 2026) MoSPI moved to a new CPI series on base 2024=100, with weights from HCES 2023-24 and the COICOP 2018 classification, replacing base 2012=100. The 2026 value is on a different basis from 2014-2025 and the two are not strictly comparable. RBI target band 2-6%.
sources.rupeeUSD: Calendar-year average rupees per US dollar: the mean of the monthly averages in the Federal Reserve's H.10 release (FRED series EXINUS), rounded to the nearest rupee. 2026 is January to September (93.9, shown as 94); 2025 averages 87.2. The record low of 96.8 is the Fed's daily rate for 20 May 2026 (DEXINUS 96.82).
sources.ssi: Constructed: SSI = sum(weight × graded severity) on a 0-10 scale, with persistence; 6 documented suppression streams incl. COVID-mortality undercount and the NSO merger. See data/compute_indices.py
sources.fci: Constructed: mean of six components on a relative 0-1 scale. Four are published fiscal ratios, min-max normalised over the years each is published: the cess and surcharge share of gross tax revenue (15th Finance Commission Table 3.8 for 2011-2018; Union Receipt Budgets for 2019-2026), tax devolution as a share of gross tax revenue (16th Finance Commission Annexure 7.1; Budget at a Glance 2026-27), states' own revenue as a share of their revenue receipts (RBI Handbook 2025-26 Table 94) and non-Finance-Commission grants as a share of Union transfers (16th Finance Commission Annexure 7.1). Two are coded: GST from 2017 and the reform-linked borrowing conditions of 2020-21. Rebuilt from these published figures on 10 October 2026; see data/compute_indices.py
sources.dqi: Constructed: geometric mean of V-Dem Liberal Democracy Index (v2x_libdem) × (Freedom House/100) × ((180-RSF rank)/180) × V-Dem Core Civil Society Index (v2xcs_ccsi); see data/compute_indices.py. The two V-Dem columns are the published series verbatim; earlier approximations that overstated the pre-2014 baseline were corrected on 15 August 2026.
sources.gigWorkers: NITI Aayog, India's Booming Gig and Platform Economy (June 2022), Table 14, gig workers in millions, usual principal and subsidiary status. 2017-2019 are NITI's actual estimates for the PLFS survey years starting in July of the year shown (2017-18 5.3, 2018-19 5.4, 2019-20 6.8). NITI's table labels 2020-21 (7.7 million) a projection, though the Ministry of Labour cites it as the current estimate, so it is held in the estimates block with the 2025-26 projection (14.3 million) and drawn as hollow markers. 23.5 million for 2029-30 is outside the site's range. NITI gives no figure for 2014-2016. NITI's 2011-12 estimate is 2.5 million.
sources.ruralIncome: NABARD All India Rural Financial Inclusion Survey (NAFIS), average monthly income of rural households: Rs 8,059 in 2016-17 and Rs 12,698 in 2021-22, a nominal rise of 57.6%. Deflated by MoSPI's CPI-Rural (base 2012=100; fiscal-year averages 132.43 and 164.53, a rise of 24.2%), the real rise is 26.8%, about 4.9% a year. Indexed 2016-17 = 100, so 2016 = 100 and 2021 = 126.8. NAFIS has two rounds only; every other year is left empty. The same survey found the share of rural households with outstanding debt rose from 47.4% to 52%.
sources.femaleLFPR: MoSPI PLFS, labour force participation rate, usual status (ps+ss), women aged 15 and over, all-India, rural + urban, from api.mospi.gov.in (retrieved 10 October 2026). 2017-2023 are the PLFS survey years starting in July of the year shown (2017 = 2017-18); 2024 and 2025 are MoSPI's calendar-year rates. 2014-2016 are left empty because PLFS began in 2017-18, and 2026 until an annual figure is published. PLFS counts a woman who helps without pay in a household enterprise as a worker.
sources.international: V-Dem Liberal Democracy Index (v2x_libdem), latest release (data through 2025; the 2026 column carries the 2025 observation forward) + RSF World Press Freedom Index 2026. Both V-Dem columns are on the SAME index: an earlier version of this table had the 2014 column on the Electoral Democracy Index and the 2026 column on the Liberal Democracy Index, which overstated India's decline. Corrected 15 August 2026.
sources.primer: Reading the Indian Economy: A Citizen's Primer (Varna Sri Raman, 16 June 2026). Figures latest available as of June 2026; several provisional, estimated, or illustrative as noted.
sources.syntheticControl: Grier & Grier (2026), 'Promises, Promises'. Figures are transcribed from the authors' published summary (rgrier88.github.io/modi-promises). Underlying data: V-Dem (governance), Penn World Table 11.0 (income). This is an external study that this project did not produce.

forecast.disclaimer: These are scenario projections, and none of them is a prediction. Each path extends the recent trend of an observed series and then applies an explicit annual adjustment for one of three scenarios. Uncertainty bands widen with the horizon because the further out you look, the more the number depends on the assumption and the less it depends on the economy. Read every projection by asking whose assumption it is and what would break it.

reform.label: Reform push
reform.desc: Statistical independence restored, garment/labour-intensive manufacturing prioritised, fiscal federalism rebalanced, formalisation incentives.

baseline.label: Current trajectory
baseline.desc: Recent-trend continuation: policy mix and institutional direction of 2019-2026 persist.

stress.label: Stress
stress.desc: External shock (oil/rupee), weak monsoon, continued informalisation and statistical opacity.

indicators.label: GDP growth
indicators.drivers: Post-COVID base-effect rebounds are fading; the level itself is contested after the 2015 MCA21 revision.
indicators.breaks: An external oil/rupee shock, a weak monsoon, or investment that keeps growing output without jobs or consumption.

indicators.label: Formal employment share
indicators.drivers: On PLFS, coverage fell from 11.5% in 2017-18 to 9.6% in 2022-23 and was 10.1% in 2023-24. Capital-intensive PLI adds output without adding much payroll.
indicators.breaks: A pivot to labour-intensive manufacturing (garments) or enforced EPF/ESI formalisation would reverse it.

indicators.label: Unemployment rate
indicators.drivers: The headline is held low by self-employment and discouraged workers; graduate joblessness runs about 13%, four times the overall rate.
indicators.breaks: A serious youth-jobs push pulls it down; a hiring freeze in a stress year pushes it up.

indicators.label: Top 1% income share
indicators.drivers: On the World Inequality Lab series the share rose from 18.4% in 2004 to 22.6% in 2022-23, the highest in a series that begins in 1922, with a dip in 2019 and 2020. No annual figure is published after 2022-23.
indicators.breaks: A wealth tax or a more progressive income tax would lower it. Without either, the trend since 2004 points upward.

indicators.label: CPI inflation
indicators.drivers: Food is 36.75% of the CPI basket on the 2024 base (45.86% on the old 2012 base), and about half of cultivated area is rainfed, so inflation still tracks the monsoon.
indicators.breaks: A deficient monsoon or an oil spike pushes CPI above the RBI's 6% ceiling.

indicators.label: Fiscal deficit
indicators.drivers: Consolidation leans on a record RBI dividend and off-budget borrowing.
indicators.breaks: A growth slowdown, a smaller RBI surplus, or new cash-transfer commitments widen it.

indicators.label: Rupee (INR per USD)
indicators.drivers: A $333bn goods deficit is offset by services; FPI outflows and a $123bn oil bill pressure the rupee.
indicators.breaks: An oil shock or sustained FPI exit accelerates depreciation; reserves can only slow it.

indicators.label: Democratic Quality Index
indicators.drivers: It is the geometric mean of the V-Dem Liberal Democracy Index, the Freedom House score, the RSF press-freedom rank and the V-Dem Core Civil Society Index, and all four have worsened since 2014.
indicators.breaks: Restored statistical and press independence would lift it; continued pressure pushes it lower.

bigPicture.note: India in five numbers. Size and income per person: IMF World Economic Outlook, April 2026. Population: UN World Population Prospects 2024 estimate for 2025, beside the government's projection for 1 March 2026 (National Commission on Population, Population Projections 2011-2036, Table 21). Growth: MoSPI Provisional Estimates, 5 June 2026, read from the economic block. Tax-to-GDP: Budget at a Glance 2026-27; the OECD average is from OECD Revenue Statistics 2025. The economy is large in total and modest per person.

items.label: Size of economy
items.sub: 6th largest at market exchange rates, 2026 (IMF projection)

items.label: People
items.sub: UN estimate for 2025; the government's projection for 1 March 2026 is 1.42 bn

items.label: Union tax-to-GDP
items.sub: Union gross tax, 2026-27 BE; the OECD average of 34.1% (2024) counts all levels of government

chinaDivergence.note: GDP per person in current US dollars. 1991 to 2020 are World Bank values (NY.GDP.PCAP.CD, retrieved 10 October 2026): in 1991 India was at $306 and China at $334. The 2026 values are IMF World Economic Outlook (April 2026) projections.

taxTake.note: For every ₹100 the Union government receives (Union Budget 2026-27, Budget at a Glance, 'rupee comes from'; rounded). 'shared' flags revenue shared with states through the Finance Commission formula.

items.label: Corporation tax
items.sub: base rate cut from 30% to 22% in 2019

items.label: GST and other taxes
items.sub: paid at the same rate whatever the buyer's income

spendSplit.note: For every ₹100 the Union government spends (Union Budget 2026-27, Budget at a Glance, 'rupee goes to').

stateReturns.note: Each state's share of the taxes the Union devolves, as set by the 15th Finance Commission (2021-26) and the 16th Finance Commission (2026-31), out of 100 (Report of the 16th Finance Commission, as tabulated by PRS Legislative Research, 1 February 2026, Table 3). Population share and income per person are read from the states block. Until 10 October 2026 this block carried a 'return per ₹100 of taxes paid' for eight states, estimated by Praveen Chakravarty for the All India Professionals' Congress; no published table behind those ratios could be found, and no government source publishes taxes paid by state, so they were replaced with the Finance Commission's own shares.

realInflation.note: Prices of different parts of the consumer basket, December 2014 against December 2025, on MoSPI's CPI (2012=100), All India, rural and urban combined (api.mospi.gov.in, retrieved 10 October 2026). December 2025 is the last month of the 2012=100 series; from January 2026 MoSPI publishes a 2024=100 index, on which headline inflation was 4.8% in August 2026 (RBI Monetary Policy Committee resolution, 7 October 2026). Until 10 October 2026 this block held a thali price from the All India Professionals' Congress and three prices described as illustrative; those were replaced with the official sub-indices.

external.note: External sector FY26 (RBI Balance of Payments releases for 2025-26; DGCI&S; PPAC; IMF WEO 2026). Goods trade is in deficit, and the services surplus offsets much of it. The current account deficit for 2025-26 was 0.6% of GDP. Goods deficit and FPI outflow are the RBI balance-of-payments figures for 2025-26 ($337.3 bn and $16.4 bn). Crude import dependence is 88.7% in 2025-26 (PPAC provisional, as reported). Petroleum crude and products imports were $173.9 bn in 2025-26 (Department of Commerce). Reserves are at end-March 2026; they were about $729 bn by September 2026.

distribution.note: Pre-tax national income per adult, 2022-23, from Bharti, Chancel, Piketty and Somanchi, World Inequality Lab Working Paper 2024/09, Table 2: the median threshold is ₹1,05,413 a year, the top 10% begins at ₹2,90,848 and the top 1% at ₹20,73,846; monthly figures are those divided by twelve. MPCE is HCES 2023-24 without imputation, a mean. PRICE's ICE 360 survey puts households earning ₹5 lakh to ₹30 lakh a year at 43.2 crore people in 2020-21.

thresholds.label: Median adult
thresholds.sub: half of adults have a pre-tax income below about ₹1.05 lakh a year

thresholds.label: Top 10%
thresholds.sub: an adult enters the top tenth at about ₹2.91 lakh a year

thresholds.label: Top 1%
thresholds.sub: an adult enters the top hundredth at about ₹20.7 lakh a year

structure.note: Output and jobs sit in different sectors. Output: MoSPI GVA at current prices, 2024-25 First Revised Estimates on the 2022-23 base (released 27 February 2026). Jobs: PLFS calendar year 2025, usual status, all India. 'Other' is mining, utilities and construction. Agriculture makes about a fifth of output and holds over two-fifths of jobs.

jobsLesson.note: Jobs per ₹1 lakh of investment by industry: Economic Survey 2016-17, Volume 1, Chapter 7, Table 2 (from ASI 2012-13 and the NSSO 68th round; investment is gross fixed capital formation). Electronics: written reply of the Minister of State for Electronics and IT to the Rajya Sabha, February 2025, as reported by ANI and The Tribune (9 February 2025); incentive released, DPIIT data as on 30 June 2026, as reported by Deccan Chronicle (25 September 2026). Central government recruitment, 2014-15 to 2021-22: Lok Sabha written answer, Department of Personnel and Training, 27 July 2022.

indexExample.note: A worked example with invented weights and prices, to show the arithmetic of an index. The weights are not the CPI's: in the real basket no single vegetable carries anything near 15%. Change the basket or the base year and the headline moves.

gdpRevision.note: The 2015 GDP revision (MoSPI, January 2015; A. Subramanian, 'India's GDP Mis-estimation', Harvard CID Working Paper 354, June 2019; Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister, rebuttal of 19 June 2019).
changes: Corporate output measured from the MCA21 database of company filings in place of the Annual Survey of Industries alone.
Sectoral output measured as gross value added at basic prices in place of factor cost, with headline growth reported on GDP at market prices.

taxReversal.note: The tax reversal (Taxation Laws (Amendment) Ordinance, September 2019, and the Finance Ministry's estimate of revenue forgone; Budget speech 2015-16 on the wealth tax; Bharti, Chancel, Piketty and Somanchi, 'Proposals for a Wealth Tax Package to Tackle Extreme Inequalities in India', World Inequality Lab, May 2024). taxToGDP is the Union's gross tax revenue (2026-27 BE); the OECD average (OECD Revenue Statistics 2025, for 2024) covers all levels of government.

budgetArithmetic.note: BE, RE and actuals (PRS, Demand for Grants 2026-27 Analysis: Rural Development; Union Budget documents). MGNREGA is demand-driven. Its spending exceeded the budget estimate in each year from 2020-21 to 2023-24 and came in just under it in 2024-25 (₹85,834 crore against ₹86,000 crore). In December 2025 Parliament replaced the scheme with the VB-G RAM G Act, 2025; the 2026-27 budget gives MGNREGS ₹30,000 crore and VB-G RAM G ₹95,692 crore. Targets: National Health Policy 2017 (public health spending of 2.5% of GDP by 2025) and the Kothari Commission (1966), adopted in the National Policy on Education 1968 (6% of GDP on education). Outturns: government health expenditure 1.84% of GDP in 2021-22 (National Health Accounts, September 2024); Centre and states together spend about 4% of GDP on education (PRS, Demand for Grants 2026-27 Analysis: Education).

kmut.note: Tamil Nadu's Kalaignar Magalir Urimai Thogai, a monthly cash transfer to women heads of household. ₹1,000 a month since September 2023; 1,30,69,831 women after the expansion of December 2024 (The News Minute). Allocation: ₹7,000 crore in 2023-24 and ₹13,000 crore in 2024-25 as reported; ₹14,414 crore in the 2026-27 budget presented on 5 August 2026 by the government formed after the May 2026 election (PRS, Tamil Nadu Budget Analysis 2026-27).

deficitFinancing.note: How the deficit is financed (Union Budget 2026-27; Ministry of Finance borrowing calendar for October 2026 to March 2027, as reported by PTI on 25 September 2026; RBI press release on the surplus transfer for 2025-26, 22 May 2026). The 2026-27 deficit is a Budget Estimate, and no outturn exists yet.

delimitation.note: Counting people allocates power. Projected Lok Sabha seat change after the first census post-2026 (Carnegie Endowment; ISAS; India Forum). Estimates vary.

monsoonChain.note: Why the monsoon moves inflation. Of a net sown area of 1,39,351 thousand hectares, 71,554 thousand hectares are irrigated, so about 49% is unirrigated (Land Use Statistics 2018-19, Rajya Sabha answer of 23 December 2022). The RBI's target is 4% CPI inflation with a band of 2 to 6%.
steps: CPI inflation nearer the 6% upper limit

cpiBasket.note: How the CPI number is built, on the CPI 2024=100 series first published on 12 February 2026 (MoSPI). Its weights come from HCES 2023-24, and it adopts the COICOP 2018 classification in place of the old six-group structure. Prices are collected from 1,395 urban markets, 1,465 rural markets and 12 online marketplaces. Food and beverages weigh 36.75%, down from 45.86% under 2012=100, so a food-price shock moves headline CPI less than it did on the old series. 'Housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels' together weigh 17.67% and transport 8.80%.

pumpPrice.note: Where the petrol price goes, as an illustration at the excise rate in force before April 2025 (₹19.90 a litre), when the Delhi price was about ₹94. Tax took about 37 rupees of every hundred. Excise was raised by ₹2 a litre in April 2025 and cut on 27 March 2026, and the Delhi pump price was ₹102.12 a litre in early October 2026 (as reported daily by The Hans India, 1 to 7 October 2026), so the current split differs (PPAC; PRS; Ministry of Finance notifications). Crude import dependence was 88.7% in 2025-26 (PPAC provisional, as reported by KNN, 1 August 2026).

modiAsks.note: The Prime Minister's appeal in Hyderabad, 10 May 2026, as reported by The Quint and Deccan Chronicle. Imports: Department of Commerce, merchandise imports by principal commodity group, 2025-26 (published June 2026). Travel: RBI Liberalised Remittance Scheme data for 2023-24, as reported by Business Standard (22 May 2024); departures: Ministry of Tourism, India Tourism Statistics, December 2024 (provisional). Crude dependence: PPAC. Rupee: US Federal Reserve daily rate (FRED DEXINUS).
asks: Avoid buying gold for one year

numbers.label: Travel remittances abroad
numbers.sub: under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme, 2023-24 (RBI); 30.2 million departures by Indians in 2024 (Ministry of Tourism)

numbers.label: Petroleum imports 2025-26
numbers.sub: crude and products; about 89% of crude is imported (PPAC)

numbers.label: Rupee (crisis week)
numbers.sub: record low, 20 May 2026 (US Federal Reserve daily rate)

gold.note: Indian households hold about 25,000 tonnes of gold, the World Gold Council's estimate (23,537 to 25,537 tonnes by September 2024, with Metals Focus, including some temple holdings). stockValueTn values 25,000 tonnes at the 2025-26 average import price of about $99,800 a kg (Department of Commerce). Account ownership: World Bank Global Findex (FX.OWN.TOTL.ZS): 77.5% of adults had an account in 2021 and 89.0% in 2024. Insurance penetration: IRDAI Annual Report 2024-25, which gives the world figure for 2024 from Swiss Re. equityParticipationPct is NSE's 13.1 crore unique registered investors (May 2026) as a share of the 2026 population projection.

poverty.note: Poverty is a contested number. Three lines give three different answers. The last official estimate is the Tendulkar line for 2011-12, and the Rangarajan report of 2014 was never adopted (Planning Commission press note, July 2013; Rangarajan Expert Group report, June 2014; NITI Aayog, 'Multidimensional Poverty in India since 2005-06', January 2024).

lines.name: Tendulkar (2011-12)
lines.detail: ₹27 a day rural, ₹33 a day urban

lines.name: Rangarajan (2011-12)
lines.detail: ₹32 a day rural, ₹47 a day urban

lines.name: NITI multidimensional index (2022-23)
lines.detail: deprivations in health, education and living standards, with no income line

bodies.note: The economy's effects show in health (NFHS-5, 2019-21, as stated in a Rajya Sabha answer of December 2024; National Health Accounts estimates for 2021-22, released September 2024).

readChecklist.note: How to read any official number.
questions: Which definition is being used, and who set it?
What does the number leave out?
When was the underlying data collected?
Who gains if the number looks good?
How does it compare with independent estimates?

measurement.note: How we know: four places where a choice of method moved the number more than the economy did (MoSPI, 30 January 2015 and the back-series of 28 November 2018; MoSPI press release of 15 November 2019 on the 2017-18 consumption survey; Union Cabinet, 12 December 2025, on the Census 2027; Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, and (Eighty-fourth Amendment) Act, 2001).

items.title: The GDP back-series
items.body: The 2015 shift to the 2011-12 base and the MCA21 corporate database raised measured growth for the years it covered, and 2013-14 went from 4.7% to 6.9%. The back-series released in November 2018 then lowered growth in the UPA years. Arvind Subramanian (2019) argued that growth in 2011-17 was overstated by about 2.5 points a year.

items.title: The survey that was not released
items.body: MoSPI decided in November 2019 not to release the 2017-18 consumption survey, citing data quality. Business Standard had reported that it showed real rural consumption falling. The next survey, HCES 2022-23, came eleven years after 2011-12 and uses a changed method, so it is not cleanly comparable.

items.title: A census a decade late
items.body: The last census was in 2011, and the 2021 census was postponed. The Cabinet approved ₹11,718 crore for Census 2027 in December 2025.

items.title: Counting allocates power
items.body: Lok Sabha seats have been frozen on the 1971 census since 1976, and the freeze ends with the first census after 2026. Reapportioned on population, populous northern states would gain seats and southern states would lose them.

states.note: Per-capita NSDP 2023-24 at current prices, 2011-12 series (MoSPI state accounts via api.mospi.gov.in, retrieved 10 October 2026; Haryana, which that table does not carry, from the Economic Survey 2023-24 Statistical Appendix Table 1.11A, as on 15 March 2024); current Lok Sabha seats (543-seat distribution frozen on the 1971 census); population as on 1 March 2026 from the National Commission on Population, 'Population Projections for India and States 2011-2036' (Report of the Technical Group on Population Projections, Registrar General of India), Table 21, converted from thousands to crore; 2011 Census population shown alongside for the comparison; total fertility rate (NFHS-5, 2019-21). 16 states covering about 90% of India's projected 2026 population and 477 of 543 Lok Sabha seats. Region is the state's zonal council under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 (Ministry of Home Affairs).
states.delimNote: Projected Lok Sabha seat change after the first census held post-2026 (Carnegie Endowment; ISAS; The India Forum). Available for 4 of the 16 states, and estimates vary considerably between them.
states.popNote: Representation here is computed on the official 2026 projection. The 2011 census is fifteen years stale and would understate how unequal representation has become. The projection is the government's own and is the best available number, but it is a projection because the 2021 census was postponed and the next enumeration is not due until February 2027. A census would replace it with a count. This project's argument applies here as well, because even measuring the fairness of a vote now depends on an estimate.

syntheticControl.note: Independent corroboration from outside this project. Grier & Grier (2026) build a 'Synthetic India', a weighted blend of comparator countries fitted to India's pre-2014 path, and measure the gap that opens after 2014. They are different authors using a different method and a different data vintage, and they reach a convergent conclusion. All values below are transcribed from the authors' published summary; none is recomputed here.

study.title: Promises, Promises: Governance and Growth in India under Modi and the BJP

income.note: The authors publish the first-year and final-year gaps and the pre-treatment fit statistic. They do not publish a machine-readable annual series. Only those published anchor values are stored here; no intermediate years are interpolated or reconstructed.

convergence.grier: Liberal-democracy gap -0.360, equal to 69.1% of India's 2013 level
Polyarchy gap -0.391, equal to 60.2% of India's 2013 level
No single counterpart; the liberal-democracy gap is the nearest
Political-corruption gap +0.272, equal to +46.8% of India's 2013 level (worse)
convergence.sp: Not separately indexed; SSI covers statistical opacity

syntheticControl.divergence: The two projects agree on direction and differ on scope. Grier & Grier make an absolute income claim, that India ended roughly $1,000 per person per year below its counterfactual, which this project does not test. The authors report that gap as larger than every placebo (p = 0.00) in three of the first four years and larger than all but one (p = 0.08) in the other seven. Some Perspective documents the decoupling of growth from employment and the concentration of its gains, but makes no claim that aggregate income would have been higher under a different government. Their income donor pool is also heavily weighted to Ethiopia (38%) and Bangladesh (25%), a defensible fit to India's pre-2014 trajectory but the part of the design most exposed to challenge. Treat the governance findings as the strongly corroborated result and the income finding as a separate, contestable claim.

eraHistory.note: UPA-decade (2004-2013) values, on the same basis as the 2014+ series so the splice is consistent. Sources: GDP growth and CPI inflation from the World Bank, which for these years carries MoSPI's national accounts (2011-12 base with its back-series) and CPI. From 2014 GDP growth is taken from MoSPI directly, with a basis break at 2023 (see sources.gdpGrowth); fiscal deficit from the Union Budget/RBI (centre, % GDP); top 1% and bottom 50% income share from the World Inequality Lab (Bharti, Chancel, Piketty and Somanchi 2024, Statistical Appendix), published for 2004-2022; press-freedom rank from RSF. SSI, FCI and DQI before 2014 are computed by the same method as the later years: the SSI from the documented record of survey timeliness, the FCI from published Finance Commission, Union Budget and RBI fiscal series, and the DQI from published V-Dem, Freedom House and RSF scores. See Methodology. Unemployment and formal/informal employment are not extended before 2014, because no annual series on the PLFS basis exists for the UPA decade. Unemployment is shown for 2015 (Labour Bureau) and from 2017 (PLFS), and formal and informal employment for the PLFS survey years 2017-18 to 2023-24.

careEconomy.note: India's two Time Use Surveys, conducted by the National Statistical Office over Jan-Dec 2019 and Jan-Dec 2024. The 2024 round covered 1,39,487 households and 4,54,192 persons aged 6 and over. Unpaid domestic services (minutes and participation) are for persons aged 6 and over; women aged 15-59 who did such work spent 315 minutes a day on it in 2019 and 305 in 2024. Employment participation and caregiving are for ages 15-59. 'Minutes' are the daily average among those who participated in the activity. They are not averages across everyone.
careEconomy.source: NSO Time Use Survey 2019 and 2024, Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (press release, 25 February 2025).

estimates._note: Published estimates and projections that are not outturns. Charts draw them as hollow markers joined to the last observed year by a dotted line; no period average, index or scorecard uses them.
